sections.h2: Lincoln as a place to sell
sections.html:
Lincoln is both the state capital and the seat of Lancaster County, and it ranks second in size among Nebraska cities. Spread over about 104 square miles, its houses differ widely in age, lot size and condition depending on the neighborhood. The combined area with Beatrice has about 372,000 residents by a 2024 estimate.

Large employers include state government, Lincoln Public Schools and the University of Nebraska-Lincoln, with Bryan Health and St. Elizabeth Regional Medical Center adding shift workers. Owners who relocate, inherit or divorce sometimes need a faster closing than a listing offers.

Lincoln mixes old and new neighborhoods, and the age of a house usually decides what an inspector will flag. Several areas started as their own towns before the city annexed them: Bethany in 1922, University Place in 1926, College View in 1929, Havelock in 1930 and West Lincoln in 1966. Historic districts sit near downtown, while newer subdivisions have spread mostly south and east.

  • Former towns such as Havelock, College View and University Place: expect questions about older wiring, plumbing and foundations on small lots.
  • Historic districts near downtown: deferred exterior upkeep and rental conversions come up.
  • South and east subdivisions: systems are newer, but the disclosure form still applies.

sections.h2: Weather and the roof, furnace and foundation
sections.html:
Lincoln has cold winters, hot humid summers and thunderstorms that sometimes produce tornadoes. Snow averages 26 inches a season. The city averages 41.8 days at 90 degrees or hotter and 10.1 nights at 0 degrees or lower.

Shingles, gutters, concrete steps and older furnaces take a beating from those swings, and an inspector will check each one. If yours are worn out, a cash sale lets you skip the repairs and sell as it stands.

sections.h2: Certificate of Compliance for rental buildings
sections.html:
The biggest Lincoln-specific rule applies to buildings with three or more rental units, not to a typical single-family home. The owner of a property with three or more residential units must give a prospective buyer, at transfer, either a valid Certificate of Compliance or a notice of Minimum Housing Code deficiencies from the Building Official.

Certificate itemAmount
First three units$90
Each additional unit$12
Fire inspection fee$70
  • A certificate is valid for 90 days from issuance.
  • Inspectors check items such as roof structure, handrails, gutters, windows, smoke detectors and electrical safety.
  • If a buyer closes without a certificate, getting one becomes the buyer's job, and code deficiencies stay with the current owner.

A Neglected Building Registry covers vacant and neglected buildings. Since June 2021, a short-term rental license costs $250 per unit and renews every year, with a cap of 10 percent of units in multi-family premises in the R-1 through R-8 districts. Hosting guests in a house you plan to sell? Look at the license status before you list. The buyer will need to sort out their own license with the city's Planning and Development Services.

sections.h2: Nebraska disclosure rules for Lincoln sellers
sections.html:
If the home has one to four dwelling units, the buyer gets a signed written statement from you about its condition. It has to arrive on or before the effective date of any binding purchase contract. Nebraska Revised Statute 76-2,120 governs, and it lets you answer "unknown" where you lack personal knowledge.

The form asks about appliances, electrical, heating and cooling, water and sewer systems, hazardous conditions, title matters such as easements, and carbon monoxide alarms. A buyer who was never handed one may sue for actual damages, court costs and attorney's fees.

Some transfers fall outside the rule. A fiduciary handling a decedent's estate is excused unless that person lived in the home, and foreclosure sales and transfers between spouses or to lineal relatives are excused as well.

sections.h2: Deeds and property taxes in Lancaster County
sections.html:
The deed is recorded by the Lancaster County Assessor/Register of Deeds Office, while the County Treasurer sends and collects the property tax bill. Nebraska's documentary stamp tax lands on the seller at recording: $3.32 for each $1,000 of value or fraction of $1,000 beginning July 18, 2026, up from $2.32. Recording also requires a signed Real Estate Transfer Statement (Form 521).

Tax is due December 31 each year, and state law lets you pay in two halves without interest ahead of the April 1 and August 1 delinquent dates. The bill pays for schools, the county, the city, fire districts and other local bodies, which is why it shows several levies.

When the house closes, expect the title company to divide that year's tax between you and the buyer. Request the parcel number early and check what has been billed so far.

Your choice turns on the house's condition, how long you can wait and what you owe. Listing may fetch more, but it brings showings, an inspection, repair requests and a financing contingency. Selling for cash to a company like ours avoids most of that, usually for less money.

  • Lean toward a listing if the house is in good shape and a few months of showings will not hurt.
  • Lean toward cash if you inherited a house you will not repair, tenants are living there, or a move date is near.
  • Test any offer against the net from a repaired, listed house after commissions, repairs and holding costs.

sections.h2: Selling a Lincoln house, step by step
sections.html:
This sequence fits a listing and a direct cash sale alike.

  1. Look up the parcel number in the Lancaster County Assessor/Register of Deeds records to see what the county has on file.
  2. Complete the disclosure form before any offer is accepted.
  3. For a building with three or more units, request the Certificate of Compliance or the deficiency notice from the Building Official.
  4. After signing the purchase contract, hand over the disclosure by the effective date.
  5. Sign the Real Estate Transfer Statement (Form 521) alongside the deed.
  6. The title company prorates tax, pays off liens and files the deed. The stamp tax is taken from your side.

Many Lincoln sellers are estates. The statute excludes a fiduciary's transfer from the disclosure form unless the fiduciary lived there, which can shorten the paperwork. You still need authority to sell, a clear deed chain and a payoff on any tax or lien. Ask the title company early what documents it wants from the estate so closing day is not delayed.

If the house is vacant, check whether it falls under the Neglected Building Registry, and keep the roof, gutters and entry points in decent shape while you decide how to sell.

Expect a buyer to ask which neighborhood grew out of which annexed town, what the roof and furnace look like after Lincoln's hot, humid summers and cold winters, and whether any part of the building is rented. If you own a house near the downtown historic districts, a buyer may ask about deferred exterior upkeep. If you own near Havelock, College View or University Place, expect questions about wiring and plumbing. Prepare short, honest answers and keep receipts for anything you replaced.

Lincoln also has a neglected building registry and a short-term rental license program, and a buyer's lender or title company may ask about either one. Having your status in writing makes these conversations short.

faqs.q: Do I need a Certificate of Compliance to sell my house in Lincoln?
faqs.a: Only if the property has three or more residential units. Owners of those buildings must give the buyer a valid certificate or a deficiency notice at transfer. A single-family house does not need one.

faqs.q: How much is the Nebraska deed tax on a Lincoln home sale?
faqs.a: $3.32 per $1,000 of value on deeds recorded July 18, 2026 or later. The seller owes it, and it is collected when the Register of Deeds records the deed.

faqs.q: When are Lancaster County property taxes due?
faqs.a: December 31 each year. The two half payments carry delinquent dates of April 1 and August 1.

faqs.q: Do I have to give a disclosure statement if I sell for cash?
faqs.a: Yes, for a home with one to four units, unless a statutory exception applies. The law applies whether the buyer pays cash or borrows. An estate fiduciary who never lived there is one exception.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Lincoln house that has a short-term rental license?
faqs.a: You can sell it. The license is issued per rental unit and renewed annually at $250, so the buyer will need to sort out their own license with the city.
